subject: ela
intro: Each problem gives you a full classroom discussion transcript with three or more speakers and competing viewpoints. You will evaluate and synthesize: choose the fairest summary of multiple perspectives, judge which contribution best advances the group's reasoning with evidence, or decide what a discussant should say next to pull differing views together. Read every turn closely and infer where each speaker stands before you answer.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about whether the school should require uniforms.
MR. HALE: Our question is, should our school require uniforms?
ANA: Uniforms could help. The article says students at uniform schools reported fewer arguments about clothing.
BEN: I disagree with requiring them. The same article notes that test scores did not change, so uniforms may not affect learning.
CARA: That is a fair point, Ben, but Ana's evidence about fewer clothing arguments still matters for how comfortable students feel.
ANA: Right, and the article also mentions families spend less when everyone wears the same items.
BEN: I will grant the cost savings, though some families say buying uniforms on top of regular clothes actually costs more.
MR. HALE: So we have reasons on both sides. Which response would be the best SUMMARY of this discussion that shows understanding of multiple perspectives?
items.answer: The group debated uniforms using the article: supporters point to fewer clothing arguments, more comfort, and lower family costs, while opponents note that test scores did not change and uniforms may add expense for some families, so the evidence cuts both ways.

steps: A strong summary reviews the key ideas AND represents both perspectives fairly, as the standard requires.
Supporting view (Ana, Cara): fewer clothing arguments, more comfort, lower family costs.
Opposing view (Ben): test scores unchanged, possible added expense for some families.
The keyed answer names both sides and the evidence each used, so it demonstrates understanding of multiple perspectives rather than reporting only one side.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about whether the town should build a skate park.
MS. ORTIZ: Should the town build a skate park downtown?
DREW: Yes. The proposal says teens have no safe outdoor space, and the park would give them one.
ELLA: I am not sure. The proposal also says the park would cost the town two hundred thousand dollars.
FINN: My uncle skateboards in the next town over.
DREW: Cost is real, Ella, but the proposal notes the park could reduce skating in the street, which causes accidents.
ELLA: That safety point connects to my worry, because fewer street accidents might lower the town's costs over time.
MS. ORTIZ: Look back at the four contributions. Which speaker did NOT contribute effectively, and why?
items.answer: Finn, because saying his uncle skateboards in the next town is off topic, offers no evidence about this town's proposal, and does not build on Drew's or Ella's points.

steps: An effective contribution stays on topic and builds on or responds to the discussion using evidence.
Drew and Ella both cite the proposal and respond to each other, even when disagreeing, so both contribute effectively.
Ella's disagreement is respectful and evidence-based, so disagreement here is still effective participation.
Finn's comment about his uncle introduces an unrelated personal fact, refers to a different town, and connects to nothing in the discussion, so it is the ineffective turn.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about a novel the class is reading.
MR. KIM: Was the main character, Tom, right to keep the lost wallet a secret?
GINA: No. The text says he 'felt his stomach twist' when he hid it, which shows he knew it was wrong.
HUGO: I think he was right, because the text says his family had no money for food that week.
GINA: I see your reason, Hugo. So maybe the book is showing a hard choice rather than a simple wrong.
IVY: Building on that, the line where Tom returns the wallet later suggests the author wants us to see growth, not just guilt.
HUGO: Good catch, Ivy. Returning it does change how I read his earlier choice.
MR. KIM: Whose turn BEST advanced the group's reasoning by connecting evidence to a new idea about the author's purpose?
items.answer: Ivy, because she points to the specific detail that Tom returns the wallet later and uses it to build a new claim about the author showing growth, extending the group's thinking instead of repeating earlier points.

steps: The best contribution advances reasoning by linking text evidence to a fresh idea, not by restating.
Gina and Hugo each give one piece of evidence for opposite first reactions; Gina then softens toward a 'hard choice.'
Ivy adds new evidence (Tom returns the wallet) and connects it to a new interpretation about the author's purpose and growth.
Hugo's reply agrees but adds no new evidence, so Ivy's turn is the one that most advances the group's reasoning.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about screen time and homework.
MS. REED: Should students be allowed to use phones to do homework?
JADE: Yes, the survey says many students look up definitions and translations on their phones.
KEN: But the same survey says students who keep phones nearby switch tasks more often and finish slower.
LIAM: So phones help with quick lookups but hurt focus. Maybe the answer depends on how the phone is used.
JADE: That is fair. The survey did separate students who used phones only for set tasks from those who kept apps open.
KEN: Right, and the focused-use group actually finished about as fast as the no-phone group.
MS. REED: Which contribution did the MOST to move the group from disagreement toward a shared, evidence-based conclusion?
items.answer: Liam, because he synthesized Jade's and Ken's opposing evidence into the idea that the effect depends on how the phone is used, which reframed the debate and led the group to a shared conclusion.

steps: Synthesis means combining others' points into a new, more complete idea, which is a high-value discussion move.
Jade and Ken offer opposing survey evidence: phones help lookups versus phones hurt focus.
Liam unites both into 'it depends on how the phone is used,' a claim that honors both pieces of evidence.
After Liam's synthesis, Jade and Ken supply the survey detail that confirms it, so Liam's turn most moved the group forward.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about a class field trip.
MR. SOTO: Should our class trip go to the science museum or the history museum?
MIA: The science museum, because the brochure says it has a hands-on lab tied to our energy unit.
NICO: The history museum, since our reading list this term is mostly about local history.
OWEN: I just think science is way more fun, so we should obviously pick that.
MIA: To connect our points, Nico, could the science trip still link to history if the lab covers how the town's old mill used water power?
NICO: That actually could work, because the mill is in our local history reading.
MR. SOTO: One speaker did not contribute effectively. Which speaker, and why?
items.answer: Owen, because saying science is 'more fun' is an unsupported personal opinion that ignores the curriculum reasons Mia and Nico gave and does not connect to or build on their points.

steps: Effective turns refer to evidence or reasons and connect to what others said.
Mia cites the brochure and the energy unit; Nico cites the reading list; Mia then poses a question that links both options.
Owen gives only 'it is more fun' with no evidence and overrides the discussion with a personal preference.
Confusing a stronger personal opinion with a supported contribution is the misconception here, so Owen is the ineffective speaker.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about recess length.
MS. PAUL: Should recess be made longer?
PAM: Yes. The article says students who get more recess pay attention better afterward.
QUIN: I worry longer recess means less class time, and the article says reading minutes already dropped this year.
RAY: What if we made recess longer but only on certain days, so we test the idea without losing too many reading minutes?
PAM: I like that, Ray. The article did say even a few extra recess days improved focus.
QUIN: A trial would let us check the focus claim and protect most reading time, so I could support that.
MS. PAUL: Which speaker's contribution BEST advanced the discussion by proposing a way to address both concerns?
items.answer: Ray, because he proposed a trial of longer recess on certain days that responds to Pam's focus evidence while protecting Quin's concern about reading minutes, integrating both viewpoints into a workable next step.

steps: The strongest move integrates competing concerns into a single proposal the group can act on.
Pam wants more recess for focus; Quin worries about lost reading minutes; they appear stuck.
Ray's 'longer recess only on certain days' addresses Pam's goal and Quin's worry at once.
Both Pam and Quin then accept the compromise, confirming Ray's turn advanced the discussion most.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about whether zoos help animals.
MR. VANCE: Do zoos help or harm animals?
SARA: Help. The article says zoos run breeding programs that saved several species from extinction.
TODD: Harm. The article also says some animals show stress behaviors in small enclosures.
UMA: Both can be true. The article notes that large, modern enclosures reduce stress, so the design of the zoo seems to matter.
SARA: Good point. So a well-designed zoo could both breed endangered animals and keep them healthy.
TODD: I will agree the design matters, though the article warns that not all zoos can afford large enclosures.
MR. VANCE: Which summary BEST reviews the key ideas and shows understanding of multiple perspectives?
items.answer: The group used the article to weigh both sides: zoos can help through breeding programs that save species, but they can harm when enclosures are small and cause stress, and the group concluded that enclosure design and a zoo's resources determine which outcome happens.

steps: A fair summary reports both perspectives and the synthesis the group reached.
Helping side (Sara): breeding programs save species. Harming side (Todd): small enclosures cause stress.
Uma's synthesis, accepted by both, is that enclosure design and resources decide the outcome.
The keyed answer captures both views and the design-and-resources conclusion, so it shows understanding of multiple perspectives.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about a homework policy.
MS. FORD: Should homework be optional?
WILL: Yes, because the data sheet shows students who choose their own practice report more interest in the subject.
XENA: But the same data sheet shows optional homework led to lower quiz averages in two of the three classes studied.
WILL: That is true. Maybe interest and quiz scores are measuring different things.
YARA: To push our thinking, what could explain why interest went up but quiz scores went down in those classes?
XENA: Good question. Perhaps students enjoyed it more but practiced less, so they were less prepared.
MS. FORD: Which turn best POSED A QUESTION that connected ideas and invited the group to elaborate?
items.answer: Yara's turn, because her question asks the group to explain why interest rose while quiz scores fell, connecting Will's and Xena's opposing evidence and inviting deeper analysis rather than ending the discussion.

steps: The best questioning move links two contributions and opens the door to elaboration.
Will offers interest evidence; Xena offers quiz-score evidence; they point in opposite directions.
Yara asks what explains the gap between the two findings, tying both pieces of evidence together.
Xena's next turn elaborates with a hypothesis, showing Yara's question successfully moved the discussion deeper.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about a recycling program.
MR. LEE: Should the cafeteria switch to all reusable trays?
ZARA: Yes. The report says reusable trays cut daily trash by half.
ABE: But the report says washing them uses a lot of water, and our town had a drought last summer.
BETH: I just feel like reusable is obviously better for the planet, so we should do it.
ZARA: Abe, the report does mention a low-water dishwasher that cut water use by forty percent. Could that ease your concern?
ABE: That detail helps. With efficient washing, the water cost might be worth the trash reduction.
MR. LEE: One speaker gave an opinion without referring to the report. Which speaker, and what should that speaker do to follow the group's rule of using evidence?
items.answer: Beth, because she said reusable is 'obviously better' without citing the report; to follow the rule she should point to a specific detail, such as the report's finding that reusable trays cut daily trash by half.

steps: The group's rule requires referring to evidence from the report before giving an opinion.
Zara and Abe both cite report details (trash cut in half, water use, the low-water dishwasher).
Beth states a feeling, 'obviously better,' with no evidence, which breaks the rule.
To follow the rule she must ground her opinion in a specific report detail, such as the half-reduction in trash.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about an article on bees.
MS. CRUZ: What is the main reason bee populations are dropping, according to the article?
COLE: Pesticides, because the article says treated fields had far fewer bees.
DANA: I think it is loss of wild flowers, since the article says bees there had less food.
ELI: The article actually lists pesticides, habitat loss, and disease together and says they combine to harm bees.
COLE: So maybe no single cause is the whole answer.
DANA: Right, Eli's point shows the article treats it as several causes working together.
MS. CRUZ: Whose contribution best reflected the FULL text and helped correct a too-narrow reading?
items.answer: Eli, because he pointed out that the article lists pesticides, habitat loss, and disease working together, correcting Cole's and Dana's single-cause readings and reflecting what the full text says.

steps: Coming prepared means referring accurately to what the text actually says.
Cole names only pesticides and Dana names only lost flowers, each a single cause.
Eli refers to the full article, which lists three combined causes, correcting the narrow readings.
Cole and Dana then revise toward 'several causes together,' showing Eli's turn improved the group's accuracy.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about a new bell schedule.
MR. DIAZ: Should school start later in the morning?
GABE: Yes. The study says teens who start later get more sleep and feel more alert.
HANA: But the study also says later start means later end, which could cut into after-school jobs and sports.
GABE: Fair. The study did note some students lost work hours.
IRIS: What if we asked which matters more for our school, the alertness gains or the lost after-school time, and looked for data on both?
HANA: That helps, because the study actually surveyed how many students hold jobs versus how much alertness improved.
GABE: If we compare those two numbers, we could decide with evidence instead of guessing.
MR. DIAZ: Which contribution did the most to turn the disagreement into a clear, evidence-based next step?
items.answer: Iris's turn, because she reframed the debate as a question about which factor matters more and called for data on both, giving the group a clear evidence-based way to decide between the competing concerns.

steps: The most useful move converts a stuck disagreement into a concrete, evidence-based plan.
Gabe values alertness gains; Hana values protecting after-school time; the two clash.
Iris asks which matters more for this school and proposes looking at data on both, connecting the two concerns.
Hana and Gabe then identify the exact numbers to compare, so Iris's turn produced the clear next step.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about a story's ending.
MS. BLAIR: Was the story's ending hopeful or sad?
JUNE: Hopeful. The last line says the character 'finally stepped into the sun.'
KAI: Sad, because just before that the text says she 'left her old home for the last time.'
LEO: Both details are there, so maybe the ending mixes loss and hope at the same time.
JUNE: I can see that. Leaving home is a loss, but stepping into the sun suggests a new start.
KAI: Agreed, the author seems to want us to feel both, not just one.
MS. BLAIR: Which summary BEST reviews the key ideas and shows understanding of both perspectives raised?
items.answer: The group found textual evidence for both readings: 'left her old home for the last time' supports a sad ending while 'finally stepped into the sun' supports a hopeful one, and they concluded the author blends loss and hope so the ending carries both feelings.

steps: A fair summary names both perspectives and the evidence behind each.
Hopeful reading (June): 'stepped into the sun.' Sad reading (Kai): 'left her old home for the last time.'
Leo synthesizes that the ending mixes loss and hope, and both peers accept it.
The keyed answer reports both quotes and the blended conclusion, demonstrating understanding of multiple perspectives.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about volunteering.
MR. WOLF: Should our grade have a required service project?
MAYA: Yes. The article says students who do service report feeling more connected to their community.
NED: I am cautious, because the article says required service can feel forced and lower students' interest.
MAYA: That is a real risk. So the way it is required might change the result.
OLA: Building on Maya, what if students chose from several service options, since the article notes choice raised motivation even in required programs?
NED: That detail changes my view. With real choice, required service might keep the connection benefit without feeling forced.
MR. WOLF: Whose turn best BUILT ON a peer's idea by adding new evidence that addressed the group's concern?
items.answer: Ola, because she built on Maya's point about how service is required by adding the article's evidence that offering choices raised motivation, which directly addressed Ned's concern about service feeling forced.

steps: Building on an idea means extending it with new evidence, not just agreeing or restating.
Maya suggests the way service is required matters; Ned worries required service feels forced.
Ola extends Maya's idea and adds new article evidence that choice raises motivation, targeting Ned's worry.
Ned then revises his view, confirming Ola's turn genuinely built on the discussion with evidence.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about a town water plan.
MS. PENN: Should the town limit lawn watering in summer?
ROSA: Yes. The plan says reservoir levels dropped to record lows last August.
SAM: Limits could hurt local lawn-care workers who depend on summer business.
TARA: My family just put in a new garden.
ROSA: Sam, the plan suggests offering those workers training in drought-friendly landscaping, which could protect their jobs while saving water.
SAM: That actually addresses my concern, because they could keep working with plants that need less water.
MS. PENN: Two speakers contributed effectively and one did not. Identify the speaker who did NOT contribute effectively and explain why, being careful not to mistake disagreement for poor participation.
items.answer: Tara, because mentioning her family's new garden is off topic and adds no evidence or response to the watering debate; Sam, though he disagreed at first, contributed effectively by raising a real concern that the group then addressed with evidence.

steps: Effective participation requires staying on topic and engaging the issue; disagreement alone is not poor participation.
Rosa cites the reservoir data; Sam raises a legitimate worker concern and then engages Rosa's proposed solution.
Sam's disagreement is evidence-based and leads to a productive exchange, so he contributes effectively.
Tara's comment about her family's garden is unrelated and connects to nothing, making her the ineffective speaker.

items.prompt:
Read this discussion about a debate on homework grading.
MR. ABLE: Should students grade their own homework?
VERA: Yes. The handout says self-grading helps students notice their own mistakes right away.
WES: I disagree, because the handout also says some students score themselves too high, which makes grades less fair.
VERA: That is a strong point. So self-grading might help learning but weaken fairness.
XIN: What if students self-grade for practice but the teacher checks a sample, since the handout says spot-checks kept scores honest in one class?
WES: That could work, because the spot-check keeps it fair while students still get the quick feedback Vera mentioned.
VERA: I agree, that plan keeps both the learning benefit and the fairness.
MR. ABLE: Which response is the BEST next move for a discussant who wants to close the discussion by reviewing the key ideas and the agreement reached?
items.answer: We weighed two sides from the handout: self-grading helps students catch mistakes fast but can be unfair when students score too high, and we agreed on Xin's plan to let students self-grade while the teacher spot-checks, which keeps both quick feedback and fairness.

steps: A closing move should review the key ideas, represent both perspectives, and name the agreement reached.
Learning side (Vera): self-grading helps students notice mistakes. Fairness side (Wes): some score too high.
Xin's spot-check proposal, accepted by Wes and Vera, resolves the tension using the handout's evidence.
The keyed answer summarizes both views and the agreed plan, so it best reviews the discussion and its multiple perspectives.
